hook: The caliph of Baghdad at its height, and hero of the Thousand and One Nights.

pages.x: Harun was born in 763, a son of the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdi, just after Baghdad was founded. As a teenager he led an army against the Byzantines all the way to the shore opposite Constantinople, and was given the title al-Rashid, "the rightly guided".

He became caliph in 786. Much of the work of ruling was done by his clever ministers, the Barmakid family, until in 803 he suddenly had their leader executed and the family's wealth seized. No one knows quite why.

Under Harun, Baghdad grew into one of the largest cities on Earth, with perhaps a million people, palaces, markets and the trade of three continents. He paid poets, musicians, doctors and scholars, and gathered a library that grew into the House of Wisdom.

Stories say he liked to slip out at night dressed as a merchant, with his vizier Jafar and his executioner Masrur, to see how ordinary people lived. These tales made him the hero of many stories of the Thousand and One Nights.

He exchanged embassies with Charlemagne, and sent him a white elephant and a brass water clock. Every hour, little balls dropped onto a cymbal to chime, and tiny horsemen rode out of doors: a machine no one in Europe could build.

He made the pilgrimage to Mecca several times, once on foot, and led raids against the Byzantines, forcing their emperor to pay tribute. He died in 809 at Tus, in Persia, on his way to put down a revolt.

Harun ruled the Abbasid Caliphate at its height, when Baghdad was the cultural capital of the world. Thanks to the Thousand and One Nights he became the most famous caliph of all, a symbol of the golden age of Islam.
pts: Ruled the Islamic world at its height
Made Baghdad one of the greatest cities on Earth
Hero of the Thousand and One Nights
